package_info.package_name: malicious executable file delivered via Microsoft Teams chat
package_info.package_manager: N/A (delivered as a Windows executable, not via a package manager)
package_info.why_malicious: The file is malicious because it is delivered through Microsoft Teams as an executable, and upon execution, it modifies the Windows registry, installs unauthorized DLL files, and creates shortcut links to establish persistence and allow the malware to self-administer on the victim's system. These actions are not expected from files shared via Teams and indicate an attempt to maintain unauthorized control over the system.

execution_context.trigger: on execution by the user after download from Teams
execution_context.file_location: malicious executable file delivered via Microsoft Teams chat (exact filename as per report, e.g., 'TeamsUpdate.exe' if specified)
required_permissions: filesystem (write access to system directories and startup folders)
process creation (to install DLLs and create shortcuts)

malicious_snippets.code_snippet: The file writes data to the Windows registry, installs DLL files and creates shortcut links that allow the program to self-administer.
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At execution-time, the code writes persistence data to the Windows registry, installs unauthorized DLL files into system directories, and creates shortcut links in startup folders, enabling the malware to maintain persistence and self-administer on the infected system.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior is suspicious because executable files received via Microsoft Teams should not modify the registry, install DLLs, or create persistence mechanisms without explicit user consent. Such actions are typical of malware attempting to maintain control over a system.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal Teams file transfers are intended for document or media sharing, not for installing software, modifying system settings, or establishing persistence. Legitimate files do not alter registry keys or drop executables/DLLs into sensitive locations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Enterprise software installers may write to the registry and install DLLs, but only during authorized installations, with user consent, and from trusted sources. These actions are not expected from files received via chat platforms.
key_indicators: Registry modification for persistence (e.g., writing to HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run)
DLL installation outside of standard software update processes or directories
Creation of shortcut links in Windows startup folders (e.g., %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup)
Executable delivered via Teams chat and executed by the user

attack_chain.action: A malicious executable file is delivered to the victim via a Microsoft Teams conversation as an attachment.
attack_chain.leads_to: Victim downloads and executes the file on their machine

attack_chain.action: Upon execution, the file writes to the Windows registry, installs unauthorized DLLs, and creates shortcut links in startup folders to establish persistence.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware achieves persistence and can self-administer on the infected system

behavioral_signatures: Executable files delivered as attachments via Microsoft Teams
Registry modifications for persistence immediately following Teams file execution
Installation of DLLs and creation of shortcut links by unknown executables received from Teams
file_indicators: Unexpected executable attachments (e.g., .exe, .dll) in Teams conversations
Newly created shortcut links in Windows startup folders (e.g., %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup)
Unknown DLLs installed in non-standard directories or outside of authorized software installations
network_indicators: Unusual file transfer activity in Microsoft Teams (e.g., delivery of executables)
Potential command-and-control (C2) communications initiated by the dropped executable after execution
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for executable files shared and executed via Microsoft Teams, especially those that subsequently write to the registry, install DLLs, or create shortcut links in startup folders. Alert on persistence mechanisms (e.g., new registry Run keys, new startup shortcuts) established by unknown executables following Teams file activity. Investigate any new or unknown DLLs installed outside of standard directories and correlate with recent Teams file transfers.
